purpose: Closed list of UK foraging species for the vision pipeline (foraging/identify.py). The vision model only picks species_ids from this list; edibility, lookalikes and the final verdict always come from this file, never from the model.
warning: Hand-curated from standard UK field-guide knowledge for a hackathon. Not reviewed by a mycologist or toxicologist. Never eat a wild fungus on the strength of a photo or an app.

edibility_levels.deadly: Can kill, often with delayed symptoms
edibility_levels.not_recommended: Not worth eating, inedible, or causes reactions in some people
edibility_levels.edible_with_preparation: Edible only when prepared correctly (cooked, seeds removed, bletted...)
edibility_levels.edible: Edible as found when ripe and correctly identified

key_features: Olive-green to yellowish or white cap, smooth, slightly shiny
White, free gills
White skirt-like ring on the stem
Bag-like white volva (sac) at the base, often buried - dig it up
species.habitat: Under oak, beech and other broadleaves

lookalikes.how_to_tell: Field mushroom has pink then chocolate-brown gills and no volva
A young death cap 'egg' cut in half shows the outline of a cap and gills; a puffball is solid white throughout

lookalikes.name: Green brittlegill (Russula aeruginea)
lookalikes.how_to_tell: Russulas have no ring and no volva and a brittle, chalky stem

species.notes: Causes about 90% of fatal mushroom poisonings worldwide. Symptoms start 6-24 h after eating, then appear to ease while the liver fails. A single cap can kill.

key_features: Pure white all over
White free gills (never pink or brown)
Ragged ring, shaggy stem
Sac-like volva at the base
species.habitat: Mixed woodland, often on acid soil, birch

lookalikes.how_to_tell: Field mushroom gills turn pink then brown; destroying angel gills stay white

lookalikes.name: Button / horse mushrooms (Agaricus)
lookalikes.how_to_tell: Agaricus have brown spore print and no volva

species.notes: Same amatoxins as death cap.

key_features: Red to orange cap with white warty flecks (can wash off in rain)
White gills, white ring
Bulbous base with rings of volva scales

lookalikes.name: Blusher (Amanita rubescens)
lookalikes.how_to_tell: Blusher flesh bruises pinkish-red; not for beginners

species.notes: Neurotoxic (ibotenic acid, muscimol). Rarely fatal but causes delirium and seizures.

key_features: Brown cap with pure white warts
Striate cap margin
White gills, ring without grooves
Bulb with a distinct rim (gutter) at the base

lookalikes.name: Blusher (Amanita rubescens)
lookalikes.how_to_tell: Blusher has greyish/pinkish warts and flesh that reddens; panther flesh stays white

species.notes: More toxic than fly agaric; fatalities recorded.

key_features: Orange-brown to tawny, often pointed (umbo) cap
Rusty-brown gills and rusty spore print
Faint yellowish bands on the stem from a cobweb-like veil (cortina)
species.habitat: Conifer woods, often with moss, Scotland and north

lookalikes.how_to_tell: Chanterelle has blunt forked ridges, not true gills, and a whitish spore print

species.notes: Orellanine destroys the kidneys; symptoms can start 2-20 days after eating. Has caused kidney transplants in the UK.

key_features: Small honey-brown cap that dries paler
Brown gills, rusty-brown spore print
Thin ring zone on a brown fibrous stem
On rotting wood

lookalikes.how_to_tell: Velvet shank has a white spore print and a velvety dark stem with no ring
Honey fungus has a white spore print and a thick cottony ring

species.notes: Contains the same amatoxins as death cap.

key_features: Conical, radially fibrous cream cap that cracks
Flesh and fibres bruise brick-red
Brown gills

lookalikes.how_to_tell: St George's has white gills, white spore print, mealy smell and does not redden

species.notes: High muscarine: sweating, slow heart, collapse. Fatalities recorded.

key_features: Small whitish cap with a frosty bloom, often in rings in grass
Gills run down the stem (decurrent), crowded

lookalikes.how_to_tell: Fairy ring champignon has widely spaced gills that do NOT run down the stem and a tough, bendy stem

species.notes: Muscarine poisoning; grows in the same rings as the edible champignon.

key_features: White cap that bruises bright chrome-yellow when scratched, especially at the stem base
Smell of ink, phenol or hospitals
Pink then brown gills, ring present

lookalikes.how_to_tell: Scratch the stem base: yellow stainer goes yellow instantly and smells of ink

species.notes: The most common cause of mushroom poisoning in the UK (vomiting, cramps).

key_features: Dense clumps on wood
Sulphur-yellow cap, darker orange centre
Greenish-yellow gills becoming purple-black
Very bitter

lookalikes.how_to_tell: Honey fungus has whitish-cream gills and a white spore print

species.notes: Gastrointestinal poisoning.

key_features: Large greyish-cream cap
Yellowish gills turning salmon-pink
Pink spore print
Mealy smell
species.habitat: Broadleaf woods on clay or chalk

lookalikes.how_to_tell: St George's has a white spore print and fruits in spring

species.notes: Severe gastroenteritis, liver damage reported.

key_features: Brain-like, lobed, reddish-brown cap (not honeycomb pits)
Cut lengthwise: cap chambered or cottony inside, not one hollow

lookalikes.how_to_tell: True morel has a honeycomb of pits and is completely hollow from cap to base

species.notes: Gyromitrin is converted to a rocket-fuel compound (monomethylhydrazine). Cooking does not make it safe.

key_features: Yellowish ball with a thick, scaly, warty skin
Cut open: firm black or purple-black inside, marbled white
No stem
species.habitat: Acid soil, heaths, birch and oak

lookalikes.how_to_tell: A puffball is soft and pure white inside; an earthball is dark inside with a thick rind

species.notes: Gastrointestinal poisoning.

key_features: Brown cap with a strongly inrolled, felty margin
Soft yellowish gills that run down the stem and peel away easily
Bruises brown
species.notes: Once eaten in Europe. Repeated meals trigger immune haemolysis that has killed people.

key_features: Chalky-white to grey cap
Red pores under the cap
Swollen stem with red net pattern
Flesh slowly blues when cut
species.habitat: Beech and oak on chalk; rare in the UK

lookalikes.how_to_tell: Penny bun has white to olive-yellow pores, never red, and white flesh that does not blue

species.notes: Severe vomiting.

key_features: Bright orange, in clumps on wood or buried roots
True sharp gills that run down the stem
species.habitat: Oak and olive wood; rare in southern UK

lookalikes.how_to_tell: Chanterelle grows singly on soil, with blunt forked ridges, not sharp gills

species.notes: Severe vomiting.

key_features: Orange cap with a downy surface
Deeply orange, thin, true forked gills
Often near pine or on woody debris

lookalikes.how_to_tell: Chanterelle has blunt ridges paler than the cap, firm white flesh and an apricot smell

species.notes: Can cause stomach upset; also a sign you may be in deadly webcap habitat.

key_features: Grey-brown bell-shaped cap without shaggy scales
Gills turn black and dissolve to ink
Often in clusters near buried wood

lookalikes.how_to_tell: Shaggy inkcap is tall, white and covered in shaggy scales

species.notes: Coprine causes a violent reaction with alcohol drunk up to 3 days before or after.

key_features: Egg-yolk yellow, funnel-shaped
Blunt, forked, vein-like ridges running down the stem (not sharp gills)
Firm white flesh that tears like string cheese
Faint apricot smell
species.preparation: Cook well.

key_features: Bun-brown cap
Sponge-like pores (not gills), white then olive-yellow
Fat stem with a fine white net near the top
White flesh that does not change colour

lookalikes.name: Bitter bolete (Tylopilus felleus)
lookalikes.how_to_tell: Pinkish pores and a dark net on the stem; very bitter

species.preparation: Cook. Discard any with maggots or soft flesh.

key_features: Very large cap (10-30 cm) with brown scales on cream
Tall stem with snake-skin banding
Thick, double, movable ring
Free white gills

lookalikes.name: Dapperlings (Lepiota spp.)
lookalikes.how_to_tell: Some small dapperlings are deadly; never pick a 'parasol' with a cap under 10 cm

lookalikes.name: Shaggy parasol (Chlorophyllum rhacodes)
lookalikes.how_to_tell: No snake-skin stem, flesh reddens; upsets some people

species.preparation: Cook. Caps only.

key_features: White cap
Pink gills becoming chocolate-brown (never white)
Thin ring
No volva
Pleasant mushroom smell; does not bruise yellow
species.preparation: Cook.

key_features: Large white ball, 10-80 cm
Cut in half: pure white, firm, uniform like marshmallow
No stem, no gills, no cap outline inside

lookalikes.how_to_tell: Small 'puffballs' may be Amanita eggs: always cut in half top to bottom

species.preparation: Cook. Only when pure white inside; discard if yellowing.

key_features: Small white pear-shaped ball covered with tiny cone-shaped spines
Cut in half: pure white inside, no gill or cap outline
species.preparation: Cook. Only young, pure white specimens.

key_features: Overlapping sulphur-yellow to orange brackets on trees
Pores, not gills, underneath
Soft and moist when young
species.preparation: Cook thoroughly; eat young edges only. Avoid any growing on yew. A minority of people react even when cooked.

key_features: Shell-shaped grey to brown caps in tiers on wood
White gills running down to a short off-centre stem
Lilac-white spore print
species.season: All year, mainly autumn and winter

lookalikes.name: Angel's wings (Pleurocybella porrigens)
lookalikes.how_to_tell: Thin pure white caps on conifer wood; linked to deaths

species.preparation: Cook.

key_features: Tall white cylindrical cap covered in shaggy scales
Gills white, then pink, then black ink from the bottom up
species.preparation: Cook within hours of picking while gills are still white.

key_features: Small tan cap with a bump in the centre
Widely spaced cream gills not running down the stem
Tough, bendy stem that twists without snapping
Grows in rings in lawns
species.preparation: Cook. Caps only. Check every single mushroom, the deadly fool's funnel grows in the same rings.

key_features: Fleshy white to cream cap
Crowded white gills
Strong mealy (flour) smell
Spring fruiting, often in rings
species.preparation: Cook.

key_features: Honeycomb cap of pits and ridges
Cut lengthwise: one continuous hollow from cap to stem base
species.preparation: Always cook thoroughly; raw morels are toxic.

key_features: Cream to pale orange cap
Soft spines underneath instead of gills
species.preparation: Cook.

key_features: Brown, rubbery, ear-shaped
Mostly on elder
species.preparation: Cook well.

key_features: Lilac to tan cap
Lilac gills
Pale pink spore print
Perfumed smell

lookalikes.name: Violet webcaps (Cortinarius spp.)
lookalikes.how_to_tell: Webcaps have a cobweb veil and a rusty-brown spore print; some are deadly

species.preparation: Must be cooked; mildly toxic raw.

key_features: Dense clumps at the base of trees or on stumps
Honey-coloured cap with dark fine scales
White-cream gills, thick white ring
Black bootlace-like strands under bark
species.notes: Eaten after thorough cooking in parts of Europe but causes stomach upset in many people.

key_features: Clusters of shiny orange caps on dead wood in winter
Velvety stem, dark brown at the base
White spore print, no ring
species.preparation: Cook; discard the tough stems.

key_features: Cream, brain- or sponge-like mass of flat curly lobes
At the base of pines
species.preparation: Clean well and cook.

key_features: Familiar apple fruit with a stalk cavity and a dried flower at the base
Oval, toothed leaves
species.preparation: Avoid eating large quantities of seeds (cyanogenic).

key_features: Small hard apples (2-4 cm), yellow-green or red
Apple-like core and stalk
species.preparation: Very sour; cook into jelly. Do not eat seeds.

key_features: Pear-shaped fruit
Glossy oval leaves on long stalks

lookalikes.name: Callery pear (Pyrus calleryana)
lookalikes.how_to_tell: Ornamental street pear with tiny hard brown fruit under 1.5 cm; not worth eating

key_features: Red to dark red cherries on long stalks in clusters
Shiny reddish-brown bark peeling in horizontal bands
Two small glands on the leaf stalk
species.preparation: Spit out the stones; do not crush or eat kernels (cyanogenic).

key_features: Oval purple, red or yellow fruit with a bloom and a single flattened stone
species.preparation: Do not eat kernels.

key_features: Round red or yellow plums 2-3 cm
Often purple-leaved in streets ('Pissardii')
species.preparation: Do not eat kernels.

key_features: Small blue-black fruit with a waxy bloom
Very thorny shrub, dark twigs
species.preparation: Very astringent raw; usually cooked or steeped. Do not eat stones.

key_features: Clustered black drupelets
Thorny arching stems
Leaves with 3-5 toothed leaflets
species.preparation: Wash; avoid busy roadsides and low-hanging fruit that dogs can reach.

key_features: Flat-topped drooping clusters of small purple-black berries on red stalks
Shrub or small tree with corky bark
Leaves with 5-7 leaflets

lookalikes.name: Dwarf elder (Sambucus ebulus)
lookalikes.how_to_tell: Non-woody plant dying back each winter, berries in upright clusters; toxic

species.preparation: Berries must be ripe and cooked; raw berries, stalks and leaves cause nausea and vomiting.

key_features: Clusters of small dark-red oval berries (haws) with a single stone
Deeply lobed leaves
Thorny twigs
species.preparation: Flesh only, usually cooked into jelly; seeds are cyanogenic.

key_features: Oval glossy red hips on a thorny climbing rose
species.preparation: The hairy seeds are an irritant: strain through muslin; usually made into syrup.

key_features: Nuts in a frilly leafy husk
Round, soft, double-toothed leaves

lookalikes.name: Turkish hazel (Corylus colurna)
lookalikes.how_to_tell: Street tree with nuts in a bristly husk; also edible

key_features: Husk densely covered in long, fine, needle-like spines
2-3 flattish nuts per husk with a pointed tassel tip
Long narrow leaves with saw-tooth edges
species.preparation: Cook (roast or boil); score the shell before roasting.

key_features: Green fleshy husk around a wrinkled nut
Leaves with 5-9 smooth-edged leaflets
species.preparation: Husk stains skin; dry the nuts before storing.

key_features: Elongated blackberry-like dark red-black fruit
Large heart-shaped rough leaves
species.preparation: Unripe fruit can upset the stomach.

key_features: Pear-shaped green to purple fruit
Large lobed leaves
species.preparation: The milky sap irritates skin in sunlight.

key_features: Russet-brown fruit with an open 'crown' of five sepals
species.preparation: Eat only once bletted (soft and brown); hard fruit is inedible.

key_features: Large clusters of small bright orange-red berries
Leaves with 11-19 toothed leaflets
species.preparation: Never raw: parasorbic acid causes stomach upset. Cook into jelly.

key_features: Small purple-black berries with a crown at the tip
Small tree, white spring flowers, red autumn leaves
Low shrub under knee height
Single blue-black berries with a bloom and a circular crown
Angular green stems
Dark green flat needles in two rows
Red cup-shaped fleshy berry-like arils with a dark seed visible in the centre
Churchyards, hedges, parks
species.notes: Needles, bark and the seed inside the red aril contain taxine, which stops the heart. Treat the whole plant as deadly.

key_features: Large, glossy, leathery evergreen leaves
Upright spikes of shiny black cherries
Crushed leaves smell of almonds
species.notes: Leaves and seeds release cyanide. Do not eat the fruit.

key_features: Thick green husk with a few short, stout spikes (or none)
Usually one large round, shiny conker per husk with a pale scar
Big hand-shaped leaves of 5-7 leaflets
species.notes: Conkers contain aesculin and saponins: vomiting, and paralysis in severe cases.

key_features: Hanging chains of yellow pea-flowers in spring
Pea-like hairy pods with black seeds
Leaves in threes
species.notes: All parts, especially seeds, contain cytisine. A common cause of child poisoning in the UK.

key_features: Glossy spiny evergreen leaves
Bright red berries close to the stem
species.notes: A handful of berries causes vomiting and diarrhoea.

key_features: Single shiny black berries the size of a cherry
A green five-pointed star (calyx) behind each berry
Bell-shaped purple-brown flowers
Large soft oval leaves
species.habitat: Chalk and limestone, woodland edges, waste ground
species.notes: Tropane alkaloids (atropine). A few berries can kill a child.

key_features: Scrambling climber
Purple flowers with a yellow beak-like centre
Drooping clusters of oval berries, green to orange to bright red

lookalikes.name: Redcurrant
lookalikes.how_to_tell: Redcurrant hangs in strings of round translucent berries from a shrub; bittersweet berries are oval and grow on a climber

species.notes: Solanine poisoning.

key_features: Upright spike of tightly packed orange-red berries at ground level
Arrow-shaped, often dark-spotted leaves in spring
species.notes: Oxalate crystals cause burning and swelling of the mouth and throat.

key_features: Climber with coiled tendrils and ivy-like lobed hairy leaves
Strings of round red berries draped through hedges
species.notes: Berries and roots are strongly purgative; can be fatal.

key_features: Twining climber without tendrils
Glossy heart-shaped leaves
Strings of shiny red berries in hedges
species.notes: Calcium oxalate and saponins.

key_features: Bright pink four-lobed capsules opening to show orange seeds
species.notes: Severe vomiting and diarrhoea.

key_features: Clusters of shiny black berries
Opposite, smooth, narrow oval leaves
Hedging shrub
species.notes: Gastrointestinal poisoning.

key_features: Round clusters of black berries on an evergreen climber
Glossy lobed leaves
species.notes: Berries cause vomiting; sap irritates skin.

key_features: Small red berries along herringbone-patterned branches
Small glossy round leaves
species.notes: Cyanogenic glycosides; mild to moderate poisoning.
